summary: This informational memo gives a framework for Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs. It aims to help standardise protocols and mechanisms by describing the significant components in a coherent way.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4110 maps the main parts and choices in provider-provisioned Layer 3 VPNs. It explains different ways to place VPN functions, discover members, route traffic, and carry packets, without selecting one solution.

subtitle: A framework for the roles, routing, tunnels, and choices in provider-run Layer 3 VPNs.

tldr.problem: Layer 3 provider-provisioned VPNs can be built using different components and operating models, so designers need a shared way to describe their main technical issues.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents reference models for PE-based and provider-provisioned CE-based VPNs, then discusses customer interfaces, membership discovery, routing, tunneling, management, interworking, and security.
tldr.outcome: This Informational framework describes alternatives without choosing a particular solution or specifying a protocol. Specific designs and engineering tradeoffs are left to other documents.

today: RFC 4110 is an Informational framework published in July 2005. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; its requirements companions include RFC 3809 and RFC 4031.

sections.title: What the Framework Covers
sections.content:
A Virtual Private Network (VPN) connects sites over infrastructure shared with other traffic while restricting communication between members and non-members. A Provider-Provisioned VPN is one in which the service provider helps manage and provision the service.

This framework covers Layer 3 VPNs over IP or MPLS networks. It uses a horizontal approach: for each technical issue it describes alternatives, but does not select a particular approach. The requirements documents include RFC 3809 and RFC 4031.
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN connects approved sites over a network that also carries other traffic. This document explains the main design choices for Layer 3 VPNs but does not choose among them.

sections.title: PE-Based and CE-Based Models
sections.content:
In a PE-based VPN, Provider Edge (PE) devices terminate the VPN tunnels and use customer IP addresses to route packets. A PE keeps a separate VPN Forwarding Instance (VFI) for each VPN it serves. Provider (P) routers in the backbone connect PE devices but do not keep VPN state.

In a provider-provisioned CE-based VPN, Customer Edge (CE) devices hold the VPN tunnel endpoints and the PE devices have no VPN-specific function. The provider manages the CE devices and may configure their routing. The two models place VPN work in different parts of the network.
sections.plainLanguage: In one model, the provider's edge devices know about each VPN and route its traffic. In the other, customer-edge devices hold the tunnels while provider-edge devices carry ordinary IP traffic.

sections.title: Customer Routing and VPN Membership
sections.content:
For a PE-based VPN, customer and provider-edge devices exchange routes using static routing, an interior gateway protocol, or BGP. PEs distribute routes among the PEs attached to the same VPN; VPN routes are not distributed to P routers. A PE may maintain a separate VFI for each VPN, including when customers use overlapping address spaces.

For a CE-based VPN, customer sites can exchange routes through the CE-to-CE tunnels, or the provider's management system can configure static routes. VPN membership information may be configured by a management system, retrieved from a directory, or distributed using a routing protocol. The framework also discusses limiting route distribution and controlling full-mesh, hub-and-spoke, or other topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: VPN members need to learn which destinations are reachable through other members. The framework describes ways to distribute that information while keeping it limited to the relevant VPN.

sections.title: Discovering Sites and Establishing Connectivity
sections.content:
The framework describes VPN setup as three logical activities: edge devices learn which other devices share a VPN, tunnels are established or selected, and routing information is exchanged. Some solutions combine these activities or use tunnels that already exist.

VPN membership can come from a network-management system, a directory server, manual configuration, or routing-protocol information. The RFC discourages relying on manual configuration because it does not scale well and is error-prone. Providers and customers may choose full-mesh, hub-and-spoke, or other topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: VPN edge devices need to identify their members, connect to them, and exchange routing information. The framework describes several ways to carry out these activities.

sections.title: Tunnels and Encapsulation Choices
sections.content:
Tunnels carry customer packets across the provider backbone. They add information used to forward a packet and can separate traffic that needs different service characteristics. The RFC discusses GRE, IP-in-IP, IPsec, and MPLS.

The approaches differ in how the receiving edge identifies the VPN, how much state intermediate routers keep, and whether they can cross networks that do not support MPLS. Hierarchical tunnels can carry several VPN-specific tunnels inside an outer tunnel, reducing the number of tunnel states needed in the provider core.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel adds a header or label so the provider network can carry a customer's packet to the correct VPN edge. An outer tunnel can carry several VPN-specific tunnels through the core.

sections.title: Management, Interworking, and Security
sections.content:
The framework addresses management of customer and provider networks, including segregated access to VPN information. It also discusses how different VPN approaches or provider networks may interwork, and how quality of service and service-level agreements fit into the design.

Security is one of the framework's design topics. The document describes considerations for Layer 3 VPN security but leaves the selection of a particular solution to other documents. It refers to RFC 3809 and RFC 4031 for related requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework also considers management, service levels, interworking, and security. Each implementation must choose and specify the approaches that fit its service.
